title: Why Encapsulation?
summary: Why public fields invite catastrophic bugs and how encapsulation acts as a protective shield around an object's data.
learningOutcomes: Explain the vulnerability of public mutable fields
Define encapsulation as bundling data with methods and hiding internal state
Demonstrate how encapsulated classes protect business rules from external corruption

activities.title: Everyday Analogy: The Medicine Capsule & Bank Vault

analogy.story:
Imagine a medicinal capsule. The delicate chemical powder inside is completely encased in a dissolvable gelatin shell. You don't scoop powder with your dirty fingers or alter the chemical ratio; you take the capsule as an intact unit.

Now consider a bank vault. Customers never walk directly into the vault to grab bundles of cash from the shelves. Instead, they stand at the teller counter or use an ATM. The teller verifies identity, validates the balance, records the transaction, and only then updates the cash balance. Encapsulation is the protective shell and the bank teller: it shields an object's sensitive data from direct, unfiltered outside tampering.
analogy.takeaway: Direct field access invites accidental or malicious data corruption. Encapsulation wraps internal variables in a protective wall and forces all interactions through verified, controlled methods.

activities.title: The Dangers of Direct Field Access vs Encapsulation

concept.explanation:
When fields in a class are declared without protection (or as public), any external class can modify them at any time to invalid or impossible values. For example, an external caller could set a BankAccount balance to -999999, set a Person's age to -50, or change an Order total without recalculating sales tax.

Encapsulation solves this by applying two essential rules:
1. Hide Data: Mark instance variables as private so no external code can read or overwrite them directly.
2. Expose Controlled Operations: Provide public methods (getters, setters, or business action methods) that validate inputs, enforce business logic, and maintain consistent internal state at all times.
rules: Rule 1: Always declare fields with the most restrictive visibility possible (default to private).
Rule 2: Never allow outside code to assign arbitrary values directly into fields.
Rule 3: Encapsulation is not just hiding variables; it is actively defending the class's integrity and invariants.

keyTakeaways: Rule 1: Always declare fields with the most restrictive visibility possible (default to private).
Rule 2: Never allow outside code to assign arbitrary values directly into fields.
Rule 3: Encapsulation is not just hiding variables; it is actively defending the class's integrity and invariants.

questions.prompt: What is the primary definition of encapsulation in Object-Oriented Programming?
questions.question: What is the primary definition of encapsulation in Object-Oriented Programming?
options: Converting high-level Java code into machine bytecode
Bundling data with methods and restricting direct outside access to internal state
Creating multiple objects using the new keyword
Inheriting behavior from a parent class
questions.explanation: Encapsulation bundles fields with their manipulating methods and hides sensitive internal state from unauthorized external tampering.

questions.prompt: What catastrophic issue occurs when instance fields are left public?
questions.question: What catastrophic issue occurs when instance fields are left public?
options: The compiler refuses to compile the class file
Objects consume double the heap memory
Any external class can write invalid, corrupted, or negative values into the fields
Constructors cannot be declared in the class
questions.explanation: Public fields allow arbitrary outside code to assign invalid data (such as negative balances or empty names) without validation.

questions.prompt: Which access modifier is the primary tool used to hide instance fields in Java?
questions.question: Which access modifier is the primary tool used to hide instance fields in Java?
options: public
private
protected
static
questions.explanation: The 'private' keyword ensures that the field is accessible ONLY within the class that declared it.

questions.prompt: If an external class attempts to read a 'private' field directly (e.g. account.balance), what happens?
questions.question: If an external class attempts to read a 'private' field directly (e.g. account.balance), what happens?
options: The program crashes with a NullPointerException at runtime
The Java compiler produces a compile-time error: 'balance has private access'
The field returns a default value of 0.0 silently
The JVM allows it if the file is in the same directory
questions.explanation: Private fields are enforced at compile time; attempting to access them from outside causes a compiler error.

questions.prompt: What is an invariant in software engineering?
questions.question: What is an invariant in software engineering?
options: A variable whose value can never be read
A condition or rule that must always remain true for an object to be valid
A method that has no return type
A loop that executes indefinitely
questions.explanation: An invariant is a core business truth (such as 'balance >= 0' or 'stock >= 0') that encapsulation strictly guarantees throughout the object's lifetime.

questions.prompt: How does an outside class safely retrieve data from a private field?
questions.question: How does an outside class safely retrieve data from a private field?
options: By using the dot operator directly
Through a public accessor method (commonly known as a getter)
By casting the object into an Object type
By calling System.out.println() on the class name
questions.explanation: Getters provide controlled, read-only windows to internal state without exposing the underlying field to mutation.

questions.prompt: Is encapsulation merely creating getters and setters for every single variable?
questions.question: Is encapsulation merely creating getters and setters for every single variable?
options: Yes, encapsulation is simply writing getX() and setX() for all fields
No, exposing uncontrolled setters for every field can be just as hazardous as public fields
Yes, Java requires every private variable to have both a getter and setter
No, getters and setters are forbidden in true OOP
questions.explanation: Blindly generating setters without validation merely creates pseudo-encapsulation. Real encapsulation enforces business rules and protects invariants.

questions.prompt: In our medicine capsule analogy, what does the outer shell represent?
questions.question: In our medicine capsule analogy, what does the outer shell represent?
options: The operating system kernel
The class boundary and its public methods
The JVM Garbage Collector
The compiler bytecode
questions.explanation: The capsule shell represents the class barrier and public methods controlling access to the internal chemical ingredients (private state).

questions.prompt: What happens if a developer later changes the internal data structure of an encapsulated class?
questions.question: What happens if a developer later changes the internal data structure of an encapsulated class?
options: All external client code in the entire project breaks
External client code continues working normally because public method signatures remain unchanged
The class becomes abstract automatically
Java requires the class to be deleted and rewritten
questions.explanation: Encapsulation decouples internal storage from external usage, allowing developers to refactor internal data structures without breaking callers.

questions.prompt: Which principle describes providing only the minimum necessary visibility to class members?
questions.question: Which principle describes providing only the minimum necessary visibility to class members?
options: Principle of Maximum Exposure
Principle of Least Privilege
Dynamic Method Dispatch
Recursive Decomposition
questions.explanation: The Principle of Least Privilege states that every component should have access to only the information and resources necessary for its legitimate purpose.

questions.question: What is encapsulation, and why is it considered the first pillar of OOP?
questions.answer: Encapsulation is the bundling of data (fields) and the methods that operate on that data into a single cohesive unit, while restricting direct access to internal details. It is the first pillar because without data protection, objects cannot maintain reliable state, making higher-level concepts like inheritance and polymorphism unsafe.

questions.question: What is the difference between data hiding and encapsulation?
questions.answer: Data hiding focuses specifically on security and privacy—making fields private so outside classes cannot inspect or tamper with them. Encapsulation is the broader architectural concept that combines data hiding with public operations, validation boundaries, and cohesive state management.

questions.question: Why is declaring all fields as 'public' considered an anti-pattern in commercial Java software?
questions.answer: Public fields eliminate all control over how and when state changes. Any part of the codebase can assign corrupted values, bypass business rules, create hard-to-reproduce bugs, and make future refactoring nearly impossible because outside code directly depends on exact variable names.

questions.question: Does providing a getter and setter for every private field truly achieve encapsulation?
questions.answer: Often called 'pseudo-encapsulation', blindly generating public getters and setters for all fields is almost as dangerous as public fields if the setters lack validation or expose mutable internal references. True encapsulation exposes business behaviors (e.g. withdraw, deposit, changePassword) rather than raw setters.
keyTakeaways: Prefer domain methods over raw setters

questions.question: How does encapsulation improve maintainability and flexibility in large codebases?
questions.answer: Because external callers interact only with public method contracts, the class author is free to modify internal representation (e.g., changing a double balance to a BigDecimal or caching values) without modifying a single line of caller code.

questions.question: What compile-time error occurs when accessing a private field from another class?
questions.answer: The Java compiler emits: 'field has private access in ClassName'. This confirms that privacy in Java is strictly enforced at compile time, eliminating runtime overhead.

practiceProblems.title: Code from Scratch: Encapsulated Temperature Sensor
practiceProblems.description: Write a complete class TemperatureSensor from scratch with private double celsius. Provide a constructor setting the initial temperature, a setCelsius(double temp) method that rejects temperatures below absolute zero (-273.15 C), and a getCelsius() method. In Main, create a sensor at 25.0 C, attempt to set -300.0 C (which must be rejected), then set 36.6 C and print 'Current temp: 36.6 C'.

practiceProblems.title: Challenge: Encapsulated Game Character Health
practiceProblems.description: Write a complete GameHero class from scratch with private String name and private int health (0 to 100). Provide a constructor setting name and full health (100). In Main, create 'Ares', apply 40 damage, apply 20 heal, apply 150 damage, and print 'Ares health: 0 (Defeated)'.
